transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-15 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~52 minutes | Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Olivia Grant (Acme Product), Daniel Park (Acme ML), Sanjay Rao (Acme Security), Priya Menon (Acme PM)

Agenda: quick intro, structured-output / JSON mode demo via API, Console guardrails and schemas, function/tool-calling integration, Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization, Q&A, next steps.

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Liam from Redwood, AE on this. We'll do a quick 45-ish minute walkthrough, leave time for Q&A. Maya and Jordan will run the demo.
[00:18] Olivia: Thanks, Liam. We're mainly interested in reliably getting structured JSON back from the model, and then calling downstream tools — inventory update, pricing, and analytics. Also security and data residency bits.
[00:32] Maya: Great, that's exactly what we'll cover. We'll show our API's structured-output mode, schema enforcement, and how function calling / tool invocation can be wired up from the Console.
[01:05] Jordan: Quick note, I might fumble some names, our transcript often says "Redwoo" or "Redood" in recordings, sorry in advance.
[01:22] Daniel: No worries, just want to make sure we can get deterministic fields back — product_id, price_delta, confidence — reliably.
[01:34] Maya: Totally. We'll demo two flows: 1) direct API call with JSON schema validation and guarded outputs, and 2) function-calling flow where Redwood returns a structured payload that triggers a downstream tool.

[03:05] Maya: Starting the API demo — here's a sample prompt and schema. "Prompt: extract price change recommendations from customer chat and return JSON." Schema has required fields: product_id (string), price_suggestion (number), confidence (0-1), rationale (string). We show the Console snippet where you paste the schema and toggle strict mode. (screen: Console -> Structured Output -> Add Schema)
[04:12] Olivia: When you say strict mode, does it reject anything that doesn't match the schema, or does it try to coerce?
[04:22] Maya: Good q. Strict mode will enforce types and required fields; we have three behaviors: strict reject, best-effort coerce & warn, and tolerant (return and mark missing). For enterprise pilots we usually recommend strict+schema tests in our eval harness.
[05:10] Daniel: How do you handle partial outputs or hallucinated ids? We need to avoid wrong product IDs getting pushed to inventory.
[05:28] Jordan: We combine multiple levers: schema enforcement, prefix KV caching for known entities, and a validation web-hook where you can run a quick canonical lookup before committing. In function-calling mode you can return an action like {"action":"update_price","product_id":"SKU123","price":12.49} and then your service can gate it behind a DB check.

[07:00] Maya: Demoing actual API call now — using our SDK: redact token in recording. Sending a request with content and the JSON schema. You can see in the Console the live parse result: green indicates schema-valid, amber for coerce-with-warn.
[08:14] Olivia: The Console output shows a confidence score — is that model confidence or Redwood's post-processed score?
[08:25] Maya: It's a combo: model token-level probabilities plus our heuristics (schema coverage, field heuristics) normalized into a 0-1 confidence. We expose both raw and normalized values.
[09:02] Daniel: Latency? We're sensitive, this will be in the critical path. If we add schema checks and webhooks, what's the p99?
[09:18] Jordan: For hosted flow with JSON mode alone, p95 for typical 100-200 token responses is ~120-180ms on our dedicated infra; adding a synchronous external webhook obviously adds the network latency — we recommend async validation for throughput-sensitive paths. If you need strict sync checks, we can talk Dedicated (reserved capacity) SLAs.

[11:45] Maya: Now the function/tool-calling part — we'll show wiring to an internal microservice. In the Console you define a function signature and mapping: name, params schema. When the model outputs a match, Redwood will return a call object, e.g. function_call: {"name":"update_price","arguments":{...}}. Then our runtime can either execute it (via a secure connector) or return to the caller for validation.
[12:30] Sanjay: How is auth handled when Redwood executes a function? We cannot give Redwood direct DB creds.
[12:42] Maya: Good point. For Private deployments we support customer-managed connectors and secrets via KMS/HSM. For Hosted we recommend a launcher pattern: Redwood returns the structured call to your service (no creds on our side) and your service executes with vaulted creds. If you want Redwood to execute, it's done via customer-provided ephemeral tokens and strict ACLs, and we keep audit logs.

[14:05] Olivia: Can we see an example of a guardrail? Something that prevents price drops below a threshold.
[14:18] Jordan: Yes — in Console you can add a webhook validation step or inline guardrail: e.g., block if price_suggestion < min_price_map[product_id] and return a flagged response. We also have prebuilt rules for numeric bounds and regex checks for strings.
[15:00] Daniel: Are those rules evaluated in the runtime or at the Console control plane? We need them to run close to the inference for latency reasons.
[15:14] Maya: Rules used in the inference path are enforced in the serving runtime — so they don't incur extra round trips to the control plane. Console is where you configure them and preview their behavior.

[17:30] Maya: Switching to Optimize briefly — we run a workload analysis and will suggest batching, quantization, and model variant to meet your p99 SLO and cost targets. For example, for high-throughput pricing updates we often recommend RPC-style short sequences and int8 quantized model variants.
[18:10] Olivia: Do you recommend client-side batching, or your runtime's automatic batching?
[18:22] Jordan: Our runtime has continuous batching that works automatically, but client-side batching helps for very small payloads to increase throughput; Optimize will suggest an ideal batch size and recommend which ops to offload or cache.

[20:00] Maya: Back to the demo — we triggered a function call and walked through a sample invocation that returned an arguments object with product_id: "SKU-992", price: 9.99, confidence: 0.88. We then simulated a downstream verification that rejected it because it violated a store-specific min price. The Console logs show the full trace and the rollback.
[22:10] Priya: On compliance, we need audit logs, SSO, RBAC, and encryption at rest with our KMS. How much of that is available for a Hosted pilot?
[22:28] Liam: Hosted has SOC 2 aligned controls, SAML/SSO, RBAC and field-level audit logs. For KMS integration and customer-managed keys we typically go Dedicated or Private, but we do support Bring-Your-Own-Key for some hosted tiers — we can follow up with exact matrix.

[24:05] Daniel: A practical question — what's the debugging workflow when the model returns malformed JSON?
[24:20] Maya: We log the raw tokens, parsing errors, and provide a replay tool in Console to re-run the same prompt with deterministic seeds and compare outputs across model versions. Also we have evals harness to run prompt sets to monitor regressions.

[26:40] Jordan: There were some small transcription typos in our previous sessions where "KV cache" got transcribed as "K V cash" but that won't affect the demo.

[28:00] Olivia: Could you walk through the integration pattern for our inventory system?
[28:12] Maya: Sure — we recommend: 1) Use structured-output schema to extract candidate actions, 2) Use a validate webhook that checks product_id against canonical store DB, 3) If valid, either return the function_call for your worker to invoke, or configure our secure connector if you want Redwood to call on your behalf. We'll diagram it in the follow-up doc.

[31:00] Maya: Quick live prompt example — sending multi-turn chat: user: "inventory for SKU-992 shows low sales, drop price by 10%?" model returns structured JSON with suggested price and a rationale. We demo different schema strictness; one output was coerced: price "9.990" -> normalized to number 9.99 and flagged as coerced.
[33:40] Daniel: How do you store policy / guardrail history? We need to prove to auditors that a rule existed at a given date.
[33:55] Jordan: Console stores rule versions and you can export audit snapshots. We also write immutable audit logs to your configured storage for Private deployments.

[36:00] Sanjay: Any penetration testing or certifications? We already have to satisfy internal infosec checklists.
[36:14] Liam: We have SOC 2 Type II report, are pursuing ISO 27001, and we publish pen-test summaries under NDA. We'll share our security pack after the call.

[38:20] Olivia: Pricing — can you share ballpark for a pilot with 100k tokens/day and a need for p95 latency < 200ms?
[38:36] Liam: We'll send a tailored pricing deck but for a short pilot we can do a usage-based setup and talk about Dedicated if you need stricter SLOs. Expect a blended per-token price plus an optional reserved capacity fee for Dedicated.

[40:00] Maya: Demoing an edge case — when the model invents a product_id, our schema-check fails and returns an error object with diagnostics. You can configure a fallback: call a human review flow. We have a built-in review queue in Console that teams can use.

[43:30] Jordan: Showing trace logs: request id, model version, kernel selection (we sometimes see "triton-opt" or internal label), batch size, and whether quantized path used int8 kernels. These are surfaced per-request for debugging. Sometimes transcripts say "Trident" instead of triton; apologies for audio typos in recording.

[45:00] Daniel: For the pilot, can we run a controlled benchmark against our worst-case prompts?
[45:12] Liam: Absolutely. Next steps: you share a representative prompt set and target schemas; we'll run the benchmark on Hosted and on a Dedicated config so you can compare latency and cost.

[46:20] Olivia: A couple of quick Qs: 1) data residency? 2) model version pinning?
[46:32] Maya: 1) Data residency is supported via regional endpoints and Private deployment; we can keep logs in your region for Dedicated/Private. 2) You can pin a model version in the route config and do staged rollouts with canary and automatic rollback policies.

[48:00] Priya: Anything we should watch out for during the pilot?
[48:12] Jordan: Pay attention to distribution of sequence lengths, tokenization differences, and fallback behaviors. Optimize will recommend quantization and batching settings after we ingest telemetry.

[50:00] Liam: Recap / next steps: 1) Maya shares demo notebook, Console screenshots, guardrail examples; 2) Liam shares pricing deck and pilot agreement; 3) Acme to send sample prompts, schema, and security checklist answers; 4) schedule pilot kickoff week of 2025-07-21.
[50:28] Olivia: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[50:35] Sanjay: We'll follow up on SOC 2 matrix and KMS questions.
[50:45] Liam: Thanks all — we'll email the links and action items.
[51:10] (end)

Notes: Transcript contains a few imperfect transcriptions and speaker label mixups typical of Fireflies exports. Shared artifacts referenced: "structured-output-demo.ipynb" (not shared in transcript), "redwood-security-pack.pdf" (to be shared under NDA), pricing deck link (to be emailed).
